newsitem.title: USA: Pavlof volcano spews ash but poses little danger.
newsitem.headline: Pavlof volcano spews ash but poses little danger.

text.p: Alaska's Pavlof Volcano spewed an ash cloud that rose to nearly five miles (8 km) on Monday but the eruption posed little danger to area towns, the Alaska Volcano Observatory said.

The volcano, located 600 miles (970 km) southwest of Anchorage, has been erupting sporadically since September 15 but has yet to cause any damage, said officials with the observatory, a joint program of the federal and state governments.
The closest settlements are the fishing villages of King Cove and Cold Bay, both at least 30 miles (48 km) away from the volcano.

Pavlof emits its ash in momentary bursts, unlike other many Alaska volcanoes, which have disrupted area towns with outpourings of ash that lasted several hours, said Tom Miller, a scientist at the Alaska Volcano Observatory.
"This kind of eruption is such that it can throw ash to reasonably high altitudes -- in this case, 25,000 feet (7,600 meters) -- but isn't sustained ash," Miller said.
Becuase of that, any ash dustings on local towns are usually "not a big problem," he said. "In some of the cases, ash has been falling in many areas and people don't even notice it," he said.
He contrasted Pavlof with Mount Spurr near Anchorage, which coated the region with about 40 million cubic meters of ash from each of three powerful eruptions in 1992.

Pavlof's continued eruptions were cause for airlines' concerns, Miller said. Observatory scientists and local pilots are monitoring the volcano for signs of ash at 30,000 feet (9,100 meters), the zone used by jets, he said.
"That's the principle hazard, to high-flying aircraft," he said.
If sucked into engines during flights, volcanic ash can cause mechanical damage and even shutdowns.
Another result of the sustained eruptions was likely to be mudflows caused by lava melting the snowpack on the northwest flank of the peak, Miller said.
"But nobody lives in there so there's no direct hazard," he said.
Pavlof's brief eruptions were forecast to continue, Miller said. "We are expecting this type of eruption for weeks and even months," he said.
Pavlof Volcano, rising to 8,242 feet (2,512 meters), is one of Alaska's most active volcanoes.
It was named in the 18th century by Father Ioin Veniminof, a missionary in Alaska who later became Saint Innocent in the Russian Orthodox faith.
